sections.h2: Where is Broomfield County and how big is it?
sections.html:
Broomfield County sits between Denver and Boulder and covers about 33.5 square miles, which makes it the smallest county in Colorado by area. It is also the newest. Wikipedia's Broomfield entry says the county was established on November 15, 2001, as a consolidated city and county, and counts it as Colorado's 64th.

The city itself was incorporated on June 6, 1961, in the southeastern corner of Boulder County. Annexations over the following decades pushed its edges into Adams, Jefferson and Weld counties, and a 1998 state constitutional amendment let the city become its own county after a three year transition. Today the county borders Weld to the northeast, Adams to the southeast, Jefferson to the southwest and Boulder to the northwest.

For a seller, the consolidation matters because one local government plays both roles. The same City and County of Broomfield bills property tax, records deeds and hears valuation protests, so most paperwork on a sale stays inside one building at One DesCombes Drive.

sections.h2: What do the Census Bureau numbers say about Broomfield County homes?
sections.html:
The figures already on this page show a county of owners with newer houses. Here is how the main numbers line up, along with the other facts we confirmed from official and encyclopedia pages.

Density was about 2,248 people per square mile in 2020, second in Colorado behind Denver. In a county that small and that crowded, almost every street has neighbors close enough to compare repairs, paint and roofs.

sections.h2: Which employers and schools shape the Broomfield housing market?
sections.html:
Broomfield's largest employers are technology, health care, aerospace and consumer brands. The county's 2023 annual report, as summarized on Wikipedia, lists these headcounts:

  • Oracle America: 1,650
  • Intermountain Health Care: 1,550
  • BAE Systems: 1,100
  • Hunter Douglas Window Fashions: 950
  • City and County of Broomfield: 900
  • Vail Resorts: 750

Crocs, Vail Resorts, Webroot and Noodles & Company are headquartered in the county. The 1990s brought strong growth in technology, and the housing stock reflects that boom.

Schools are split six ways: Boulder Valley, 27J, Weld County RE-8, Jefferson County, St. Vrain Valley and Adams 12 Five Star. Two houses a few blocks apart can feed different districts, so buyers ask which one applies. That is worth writing down before you list or accept an offer.

sections.h2: How does the Broomfield County property tax calendar work?
sections.html:
Broomfield property tax can be paid in full by April 30, or in two halves due February 28 and June 15. These dates come from the Treasurer's page, which says taxes paid by those dates carry no interest.

The Treasurer lists a 2.50% provider fee for credit card payments and a $2.50 fee for eCheck. Online payments are limited to $1,000,000 per transaction. Taxes under $25 must be paid with the full-year option. The page also notes that a postmark confirms the date the mail was held, not necessarily the day it was dropped off, so it suggests asking the postal clerk for a manual postmark.

Payment optionDue date
First halfFebruary 28
Second halfJune 15
Full yearApril 30

Late payments carry a charge that grows by month. The Treasurer's chart shows 1% for a first-half payment made in March and 2% in April. The property tax information page describes the penalty as 1% interest per month after the due dates.

The tax notice goes to the owner of record, not to the mortgage company. If a lender escrows your taxes, the page says to check with the lender about who pays.

sections.h2: Who sets the value on a Broomfield County house?
sections.html:
The Assessor sets value and the Treasurer collects the tax. The property tax page puts it plainly: assessors do not set tax rates or chase tax dollars. Local mill levies come from taxing authorities such as school districts and fire districts.

The Assessor is reachable at assessor@broomfield.org or 303-464-5819. The valuation process page says reappraisals happen in odd numbered years, with the assessment date set at January 1. Sales from a 24 month window feed the model, and for the 2025 reappraisal the page lists July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024. In even numbered years values stay put unless new construction, finished basements, additions or demolitions change them.

Residential property must be valued with the market approach, which compares sales of similar homes. The office has published single family and condo sales lists for the 2025 reappraisal, which you can use as a starting point if your value looks high.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Broomfield County property valuation?
sections.html:
You file a protest with the Assessor between May 1 and June 8 for real property. The appeal information page accepts filings three ways:

  • Online through the appeal portal, which has a neighborhood sales map and document upload.
  • By mail to Broomfield County Assessor, PO Box 1149, Broomfield, CO 80038-1149, postmarked by June 8.
  • In person at the Community Assistance Center in the lobby of the George Di Ciero City and County Building.

Useful evidence includes an appraisal dated within the sales window, photos of condition, comparable sales and proof of any error in the property record. A Notice of Determination follows by June 30 for real property.

If you disagree, the next step is the Board of Equalization. Real property filings are due July 15, and the Board of Equalization page says hearings are held remotely by Google Meet, with an independent hearing officer. You can choose up to five comparable sales online, new evidence is due at least three days before the hearing, and hearings cannot be rescheduled. Questions go to clk-boe@broomfield.org or 303-438-6332, option 9.

An appeal helps most when you plan to keep the house. If you are selling, the lower value only helps the year you own it, so many sellers weigh the effort against the closing date.

sections.h2: What happens if the property tax goes unpaid in Broomfield County?
sections.html:
Unpaid real estate tax ends up at a public tax lien sale. Broomfield's tax lien sale page says the sale is usually held in November, and the 2026 sale was set for November 4, 2026 at 9 a.m. in the City Council Chamber.

Buyers purchase a lien, not the property. The page describes a three year redemption period for most properties, during which the house still belongs to the assessed owner, and says very few liens actually go to deed. The rate on certificates sold in 2026 is thirteen percent, and liens not sold at the sale stay with the county.

  • The list of delinquent taxes is advertised for three consecutive weeks before the sale.
  • Bidders may offer premiums above the tax due, and premiums are not refunded when the lien is redeemed.
  • Redeeming means paying the tax, interest and fees, which usually happens at or before a sale of the house.

An owner behind on tax can still sell. The title company pays the back tax out of proceeds and the lien clears at closing.

sections.h2: What does a seller need to know about taxes due at closing in Broomfield County?
sections.html:
Title companies usually ask for a Certificate of Taxes Due before closing. The Treasurer describes it as a certification that all taxes are paid except those shown as still due, and cites C.R.S. 39-10-115. If a tax was omitted from the certificate, Broomfield says it will take care of the omitted amount.

Colorado tax is paid in arrears, so a sale in the middle of a year leaves the seller owing a share of the bill that has not been issued yet. Your closing statement will show how that share is split. Ask for the line items early.

Out of state owners have one more step. When a nonresident sells Colorado real property, the Department of Revenue says the closing agent generally withholds the lesser of 2% of the sales price or the net proceeds and sends it in on form DR 1079. The seller can claim it back on a Colorado return if it exceeds the tax owed. See the Department of Revenue guidance.

sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Broomfield County?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded by the Recording Division at One DesCombes Drive, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. except holidays. Phone 303-464-5109 or email RecordingInformation@broomfield.org. The recording page lists these terms:

  • A $40 flat fee for any number of pages, plus a $3 surcharge per document, effective July 1, 2025.
  • One inch margins at the top and bottom and half inch margins on the sides.
  • A cover sheet with contact information and payment for drop off or mail.
  • E-recording for most documents through the self service portal.

Records from November 2001 forward are searchable online. For older records, the office points to Adams, Boulder, Jefferson or Weld County, because the land came from those counties.

sections.h2: What do sellers in Broomfield County usually run into?
sections.html:
The common snags are tax status, older records and house condition. Houses built around 2001 are now reaching the age where roofs, water heaters and windows need work, and a Front Range hail season is hard on roofs. Wikipedia's Colorado entry notes that hailstorms hit Denver in 1990 and on May 8, 2017, the latter being the costliest in state history.

The state's wildfire history matters to insurers and buyers too. The same entry calls the Marshall Fire of December 30, 2021 the most destructive in Colorado in terms of property loss. Ask your insurer what it requires before a buyer's lender asks.

If you would rather skip repairs and showings, a cash sale as-is removes most of those steps. We buy Broomfield County houses as they stand and can work around tax balances, inherited title and tenants. The page above shows what a county contact can verify on your parcel.

faqs.q: When is Broomfield County property tax due?
faqs.a: Broomfield property tax is due in full by April 30, or in halves on February 28 and June 15. Payments by those dates carry no interest, according to the Treasurer's page.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Broomfield County property tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Treasurer's office at 303-464-5810 for billing, or email treasurer@broomfield.org. Valuation questions go to the Assessor at 303-464-5819.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to protest a Broomfield County valuation?
faqs.a: For real property, the protest window runs from May 1 to June 8, and mailed forms must be postmarked by June 8. A Board of Equalization appeal of the Assessor's decision is due July 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Broomfield County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Back tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing and the title company clears the lien. Unpaid taxes can otherwise go to the November tax lien sale.

faqs.q: Does Broomfield County have a separate county recorder?
faqs.a: Broomfield is a consolidated city and county, so one local government handles recording through its Recording Division at One DesCombes Drive. Fees from July 1, 2025 are $40 plus a $3 surcharge per document.
